title: Open and Reproducible Science in R
text:
Welcome
This book contains the Open and Reproducible Science in R workshop materials. In 90 minutes, we follow the HealthWellbeing dataset through an end-to-end reproducible research workflow. We start with Git and GitHub, including a short activity in which you read the workshop’s history. Short demonstrations then cover computational environments, FAIR metadata, and data and model versioning. In the hands-on exercises, you complete and run a targets meta-analysis pipeline, render a Quarto report from its outputs, then change the analysis and reproduce the results. We finish with releases, archiving, and discussion. A supplementary exercise covers synthetic data with synthpop.

15.1.1 Abstract / description
Open and reproducible science helps others understand, evaluate, and reuse research. This 90-minute workshop follows one prepared R project through that workflow.
We start with Git and GitHub, including a short activity in which you read the workshop’s history. Short demonstrations then cover reproducible environments with renv, Docker, and MyBinder, FAIR metadata and assessment with dataspice and rfair, and data and model versioning with pins and vetiver. In the hands-on exercise, you will complete and run a targets meta-analysis pipeline, render its Quarto report, and change an analysis setting to see which steps rebuild. We close by working out what to include in a GitHub release and Zenodo archive.
You will use public teaching data in a prepared browser session. Allow time to follow the preparation steps before the workshop. Basic familiarity with R will help.

title: 18  Accessibility
text:
18.1 Accessibility goals
For web content and interfaces, we work toward WCAG 2.2 Level AA. This is a development goal; any claim of conformance must be supported by an evaluation that identifies its scope, date, methods, findings, and remaining limitations.
Across the project, we prioritise:

title: 18  Accessibility
text:
Clear language, descriptive links, and a logical content structure.
Keyboard access and visible focus for interactive interfaces.
Meaningful labels, headings, and semantics for assistive technologies.
Readable content that works with zoom, different screen sizes, and user settings.
Equivalent ways to understand information presented through images, colour, audio, video, or interaction.
Clear instructions, actionable errors, and accessible examples and outputs.

title: 18  Accessibility
text:
18.2 Contributor expectations
Consider accessibility when adding or changing user-facing content or behaviour. Apply these practices where relevant:

Use a logical heading hierarchy, semantic lists, and descriptive link text.
Provide useful alternative text for informative images. For complex figures, include a nearby explanation or an accessible table of the relevant data. See the W3C alternative-text decision tree.
Give tables appropriate headers and explain units, abbreviations, and symbols.
Use sufficient contrast and additional cues alongside colour to convey meaning.
Provide captions for video and transcripts for audio, with descriptions of essential visual information where needed.
Keep text and controls usable with zoom and on narrow screens.
Give controls accessible names and states. Keep focus order logical, make actions work with a keyboard, and avoid keyboard traps.
Declare the language of web content and identify changes of language when needed.
Make instructions, code examples, command-line help, and error messages clear and usable without relying solely on screenshots or visual layout.


18.2.1 Reviewing changes
Use existing project checks where available. For affected interfaces, combine automated checks with manual keyboard testing and, where possible, checks with assistive technology. Automated tools cover only part of an accessibility review.
In a pull request, describe what was checked, the tools and environments used, any barriers found, and any checks that could not be completed. Record unresolved issues and workarounds so maintainers can assess their impact. Introduce or change automated checks through the project’s normal contribution process.

title: 18  Accessibility
text:
18.3 Reporting an accessibility barrier
Open an issue in the repository’s issue tracker. Use an accessibility template or label if one is available; a general issue is also welcome. If the tracker is unavailable or difficult to use, use a contact or support route documented in the repository’s README.
Include whatever information you can comfortably provide:

The task you were trying to complete and the barrier you encountered.
The affected page, file, command, feature, or output, including a version if known.
Steps to reproduce the problem and what you expected to happen.
Relevant browser, operating system, device, or assistive technology details.
The impact on your work and any workaround you have found.

Screenshots and recordings are optional. You do not need to disclose a disability, diagnosis, or other personal information to report a barrier or request help. Avoid including confidential data or credentials in a public report.

title: 18  Accessibility
text:
18.4 Prioritisation and response
Repository maintainers coordinate accessibility work and may delegate individual issues to contributors. Reports should be acknowledged respectfully and assessed according to their effect on users’ ability to complete tasks.
Prioritise barriers that prevent essential tasks or have no practical workaround. Consider the number of affected users, available alternatives, dependencies, and the effort needed to address an issue. Reporters do not need to assign a severity.
Track agreed next steps and, where possible, provide workarounds and progress updates. Set response or resolution targets only when the project can support them, and communicate changes to an agreed timeline. Invite feedback on whether a proposed fix resolves the reported barrier.

title: 18  Accessibility
text:
18.5 Tested environments and known limitations
Record the browsers, devices, assistive technologies, software versions, and output formats actually checked in project documentation, issues, or pull requests. Describe the scope and date of testing when reporting compatibility.
Document confirmed barriers with their user impact, affected versions, known workarounds, and follow-up work. Identify relevant limits in third-party tools or embedded content. Revisit these records as the project and its dependencies change.

title: 18  Accessibility
text:
18.6 Maintaining this policy
Maintainers should review this policy when user-facing features, support routes, or accessibility practices change. Suggestions and corrections are welcome through the repository’s usual contribution and support channels.

title: 19  Security Policy
text:
If you discover a security vulnerability in this project, we encourage you to let us know right away. Please report security issues to us by creating a new security advisory.
The following information will help us triage your report more quickly:

Type of issue (e.g. buffer overflow, SQL injection, cross-site scripting, etc.)
Full paths of source file(s) related to the manifestation of the issue
The location of the affected source code (tag/branch/commit or direct URL)
Any special configuration required to reproduce the issue
Step-by-step instructions to reproduce the issue
Proof-of-concept or exploit code (if possible)
Impact of the issue, including how an attacker might exploit the issue

title: 20  AI-assisted development policy
text:
20.1 Responsibility and review
Contributors remain responsible for the accuracy and suitability of the work they submit. AI-generated contributions follow the same review and acceptance process as other contributions. A human contributor must take responsibility for the submission and complete any human review required by the project.
State whether human review is complete or pending. Agent-run checks and automated reviews provide evidence for reviewers; they do not constitute human review.

title: 20  AI-assisted development policy
text:
20.2 Agent scope and authorisation
Agents may implement assigned tasks, run appropriate checks, prepare changes, and carry out other actions covered by the contributor’s instructions. Follow repository-specific guidance, including agent instructions, contribution rules, and security policies where these are provided.
Respect the task’s scope and preserve existing work. A review-only request does not authorise edits. Keep unrelated changes separate, and identify assumptions or missing information that materially affect the work.
Commits, external messages, merges, deployments, releases, and other shared changes must follow the contributor’s authorisation and the project’s approval process. Existing authorisation applies to actions within its scope. Do not infer permission to perform unrelated or destructive actions from access to a tool.

title: 20  AI-assisted development policy
text:
20.3 Disclosing material AI assistance
Disclose material AI assistance where the work is submitted, such as a pull request description, issue, review, or other contribution record. Briefly state:

Which tool or service was used and what it helped produce or review.
Which checks were performed and their results.
Remaining limitations and whether human review is complete or pending.

For example: “An AI coding assistant helped implement the change. Unit tests pass; integration testing and human review are pending.”
Keep disclosure relevant to the contribution. Full chat transcripts, prompts, and large blocks of raw output are not required. Review any material shared publicly for confidential information or credentials.

title: 20  AI-assisted development policy
text:
20.4 Verification and evidence
Check generated code, explanations, references, and API usage against the project’s actual environment and appropriate sources. Do not invent results, citations, provenance, test outcomes, or security and privacy guarantees. Distinguish proposed work from implemented and verified behaviour.
Run checks appropriate to the change. Report failures, skipped checks, missing dependencies, and untested environments accurately. Syntax checks, tests, builds, rendered documents, and executed workflows provide different evidence; identify which checks actually ran and what they establish.
For work involving data, models, or analytical results, preserve source inputs and record the versions, parameters, transformations, and environment needed to understand or reproduce the result. Explain substantive assumptions and use appropriate validation for the project’s domain.
Keep dependency changes deliberate and review generated files and configuration for effects beyond the assigned task. Follow the project’s established testing, formatting, accessibility, and review practices.

title: 20  AI-assisted development policy
text:
20.5 Data protection and confidentiality
Use only data and services approved for the task. Share the minimum context needed, and check applicable organisational rules, data-owner permissions, and service settings before providing non-public material to an external AI service.
Do not expose credentials, personal information, confidential code, or restricted data through prompts, logs, generated examples, or contribution records. Use public, synthetic, or redacted examples where appropriate, and verify that the chosen example is suitable for sharing.

title: 20  AI-assisted development policy
text:
20.6 Licensing and provenance
Respect software licences, copyright, and attribution requirements when using AI-generated material or adapting suggested code and text. Verify source and licensing information when it affects whether an output can be included. Preserve required notices and document relevant sources or adaptations.

title: 20  AI-assisted development policy
text:
20.7 Contributions and concerns
Follow the repository’s contribution and conduct policies where available. Report suspected vulnerabilities or disclosures of sensitive information through the project’s documented security or private reporting route. Use the normal support or issue channels for other questions about AI-assisted contributions.
Maintainers should update this policy as the project’s tools, risks, and review practices change. Project-specific requirements may supplement this policy and should be documented alongside it.

1.1 About the workshop
Open and reproducible science helps others understand, evaluate, reuse, and extend research. In this 90-minute workshop, we follow one prepared R project from its source data to an archived result.
The workshop is presented by James Bristow, Massey University, with co-author Hana Liang, Bioeconomy Science Institute.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 Learning objectives
By the end of the workshop, participants should be able to:

Explain how the tools support different parts of a reproducible research workflow.
Use FAIR principles to document variables, provenance, licensing, and access conditions, and interpret an automated assessment.
Explain how pins and vetiver link results to specific data and model versions.
Complete and run a targets pipeline and render a Quarto report from its outputs.
Change an analysis setting, rebuild only what is affected, and reproduce the result.
Identify the files and metadata needed for a citable release and archive.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.5 Principles to put into practice
Throughout the session, consider whether another researcher could:

Understand the purpose of the project and follow the analysis decisions.
Reproduce the environment and rerun the workflow on another machine.
Audit the history of changes and the relationship between inputs and outputs.
Trace a reported result to the versions of its data, fitted model, and software environment.
Reuse and extend the code and materials with clear documentation and licensing.
Assess sharing limits and distinguish a runnable workflow from verification of restricted-data findings.
Find and cite a preserved version of the research outputs.

We will consider common barriers to these goals, including undocumented dependencies, manual analysis steps, and assumptions tied to a single computing environment.

title: 5  Introduction, reproducibility principles, Git and GitHub
text:
5.2 Why this matters
A reported result is easier to evaluate when its data, analytical decisions, code, and software environment can be traced. Sharing code helps, but the code also needs identifiable inputs and instructions that work beyond its author’s current R session.
In this workshop, reproducibility means being able to rerun a documented workflow with its specified inputs and environment. Open science also concerns how methods and outputs can be inspected, accessed, and reused. Throughout the session, ask whether another researcher could understand, rerun, audit, trace, reuse, and cite the work.

section: 5.5 Version control with Git and GitHub
text:
5.5 Version control with Git and GitHub
Git records the history of a project’s files. GitHub hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration tools such as issues, pull requests, and releases.







Term
Meaning




Commit
A recorded change to one or more files, with a message explaining why


Branch
A line of work that can change without affecting the main version


Remote
A copy of the repository elsewhere, such as on GitHub


Push
Send local commits to a remote repository


Pull request
A proposal to merge a branch, with a place for review and discussion


Release
A named, tagged version of the repository, covered later in the session




5.5.1 Read the workshop’s history
The project in your MyBinder session is a copy of the files without their Git history, but Git can read the history of the public repository directly.

Which versions have been released? List the repository’s tags without downloading anything else.


url=https://github.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r.git
git ls-remote --tags --refs "$url"

Each line pairs a commit hash with a version tag. A tag gives one commit a permanent name. We will later cover how Zenodo archives each tagged release with its own DOI.

What changed recently, and why? Copy the history into a temporary folder. --filter=blob:none fetches the commits and the lists of files they changed, but not the file contents, so it takes a few seconds.


rm -rf /tmp/workshop-history.git
url=https://github.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r.git
git clone --quiet --bare --filter=blob:none "$url" /tmp/workshop-history.git
git -C /tmp/workshop-history.git log --oneline --no-merges -5
git -C /tmp/workshop-history.git log --oneline -3 -- pipelines/_targets_health_wellbeing.R

The first log lists the latest changes, and each message says what changed. The second lists only the commits that changed the reference pipeline.

Is the reference pipeline in your session the latest version? Git identifies each version of a file by a hash of its contents. Compare the copy in your MyBinder project with the one in the latest commit.


git hash-object pipelines/_targets_health_wellbeing.R
git -C /tmp/workshop-history.git rev-parse HEAD:pipelines/_targets_health_wellbeing.R

Matching lines mean identical contents. If they differ, the repository changed after your MyBinder environment was built. This is why a result should cite a specific commit or release rather than “the latest version”.

text:
6.2 Why this matters
The same script can behave differently when package versions or system libraries change. We need to describe the environment alongside the code and the data version.

What we record

renv restores the R packages described by a lockfile. A Docker image can also include the R interpreter, operating-system libraries, and rendering tools. Binder starts a container from such an image in a browser.

title: 6  Computational reproducibility
text:
6.3 Inspect the R environment
We can next view the contents of the renv.lock file:

file.edit("renv.lock")

The version of R running with your environment should ideally match the lock file.

source("pipelines/workshop_support.R")
use_workshop_book_outputs()

R.version.string

[1] "R version 4.4.1 (2024-06-14)"

packageVersion("renv")

[1] '1.0.7'


Compare the running version with the reference version, 4.4.1. A lockfile records a version; it does not switch your running R session.

lock <- renv::lockfile_read("renv.lock")
lock$R$Version

[1] "4.4.1"

workshop_packages <- c(
  "dataspice", "meta", "pins", "rfair", "rmarkdown",
  "synthpop", "targets", "vetiver"
)
vapply(
  workshop_packages,
  function(package) {
    record <- lock$Packages[[package]]
    if (is.null(record)) NA_character_ else record$Version
  },
  character(1)
)

dataspice      meta      pins     rfair rmarkdown  synthpop   targets   vetiver 
  "1.2.1"   "9.0-0"   "1.4.2"   "0.2.0"    "2.32"   "1.9-3"  "1.12.0"   "0.2.8" 

renv::status()

No issues found -- the project is in a consistent state.


The lockfile records exact package versions for the workshop. renv::status() checks whether the active library matches the lockfile.
The usual collaboration cycle is:

A maintainer prepares and tests the required packages.
The maintainer uses renv::snapshot() and reviews the resulting lockfile.
Collaborators use renv::restore() to obtain the recorded packages.
The analysis is tested in the restored environment.

The workshop’s Binder image was built by restoring this lockfile, so you do not need to run renv::restore() during the session.

Instruction
What it does in this project

Starts from Rocker’s Binder image for R 4.4.1.

Executes build steps such as installing system libraries and restoring R packages from renv.lock.

A Docker build uses these instructions and the repository files to produce an image. A container is a running instance of an image. Each participant runs the workshop in their own container started from the same image.

Principle
Ask
Example for this dataset




Findable
Can someone locate and identify it?
A named record with a stable identifier and searchable metadata.


Accessible

text:
7.3 Assess the snapshot with rfair
rfair takes a URL or persistent identifier and applies a set of tests to the metadata it can retrieve (Sofi-Mahmudi 2026).
First, assess the HealthWellbeing.rda file:

metadata_file <- file.path("data", "metadata", "health-wellbeing", "dataspice.json")
metadata <- jsonlite::read_json(metadata_file)
snapshot_url <- metadata$distribution[[1L]]$contentUrl
baseline <- rfair::assess_fair(
  snapshot_url, metric_version = "0.8", timeout = 6, max_time = 30
)
baseline

<fair_assessment> https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MathiasHarrer/dmetar/38c9b9bb5f85ea49de33e5d2536f6544d5268517/data/HealthWellbeing.rda
  resolved: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MathiasHarrer/dmetar/38c9b9bb5f85ea49de33e5d2536f6544d5268517/data/HealthWellbeing.rda
  metrics: v0.8 (17 metrics)

  FAIR     earned  percent  maturity
  F           1/7    14.3%         1
  A           2/7    28.6%         2
  I           0/6     0.0%         0
  R           0/6     0.0%         0
  FAIR       3/26    11.5%         1
  id hygiene: 1 issue(s) (see $identifier_hygiene)


We will next assess the JSON-LD file:

metadata_url <- paste0(
  "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r@",
  "c08e0dc036e46e89376536a87ad279db61374f7e",

enriched <- rfair::assess_fair(
  snapshot_url,
  metric_version = "0.8",
  metadata_service_endpoint = metadata_url,
  metadata_service_type = "schema_org",
  timeout = 6,
  max_time = 30
)

  metrics: v0.8 (17 metrics)

And follow up with a comparison of the original evaluation against this new evaluation:

comparison <- rfair::fair_compare(baseline, enriched)
metrics <- c("FsF-F1-02MD", "FsF-A1-01M", "FsF-I1-01M", "FsF-R1.1-01M")
comparison[comparison$metric_identifier %in% metrics,
           c("metric_identifier", "status_a", "status_b")]

   metric_identifier status_a status_b
2        FsF-F1-02MD     fail     fail
6         FsF-A1-01M     fail     fail
10        FsF-I1-01M     fail     pass
14      FsF-R1.1-01M     fail     pass


One metric from each principle shows what changed and what stayed the same.



Metric
Download URL alone
With the JSON-LD supplied




Persistent identifier (FsF-F1-02MD)
Fail
Fail


Access information in metadata (FsF-A1-01M)
Fail
Fail


Formal language for metadata (FsF-I1-01M)
Fail
Pass


Licence in metadata (FsF-R1.1-01M)
Fail
Pass



The file downloaded successfully in both runs, yet the access check (FsF-A1-01M) failed both times. Why? What would you add to the public record so a reader knows how to get the file?






One possible answer





This metric looks for access information in the metadata. A working link shows that the assessor could download the file at that moment. It does not tell a reader whether anyone can download it, whether they need to sign in, or whether they must request approval.
For this snapshot, a statement such as “Public download, no sign-in required” beside the URL would answer the question. Schema.org has isAccessibleForFree and conditionsOfAccess properties for this. For a restricted dataset, the record could say who may access the data and how to request it. Rerun the assessment to check whether a particular metric version recognises the statement.

text:
8.3 Store model versions with vetiver
We have assessed whether our dataset adheres to FAIR principles and we have also versioned it. We can next do some statistical modelling. Typically, we might want to use a mixed-effects model to perform a meta-analysis, but for the purposes of this demonstration we shall fit a linear regression model of Fisher z (atanh(cor)) against log sample size, then store it with vetiver.
We will first process the data.

health_full <- pin_read(
  data_board, "health_wellbeing", version = full_version
)

original <- data.frame(
  population = factor(health_full$population),
  z = atanh(health_full$cor),
  log_n = log(health_full$n)
)
head(original, 5)

          population         z     log_n
1 general population 0.7250051  4.795791
2  chronic condition 0.3907423  5.948035
3 general population 0.2985663 12.765688
4 general population 0.3461986  7.475339
5 general population 0.9287274 10.653275


Subsequently, we fit and save a linear regression.

lm_model <- stats::lm(z ~ log_n, data = original)

v_model <- vetiver_model(lm_model, model_name = "health_wellbeing_lm")
vetiver_pin_write(board, v_model)

We will next reload the model from a vetiver pin. Its input prototype lists the columns required for prediction. Its metadata records the training data version and hash.

version_file <- file.path(workshop_dir, "predictive-model-version.txt")
model_version <- readLines(version_file, warn = FALSE)
model_board <- pins::board_folder(file.path(workshop_dir, "model_store"), versioned = TRUE)
model_lm <- vetiver::vetiver_pin_read(
  model_board, "health_wellbeing_lm", version = model_version
)
tibble::tibble(
  name = model_lm$model_name,
  description = model_lm$description,
  version = model_lm$metadata$version,
  recipe = model_lm$metadata$user$recipe,
  r_version = model_lm$metadata$user$r_version,
  vetiver_version = model_lm$metadata$user$vetiver_version

title: 9  Build and execute a targets meta-analysis pipeline
text:
9.2 The pipeline at a glance
A target is one named step whose result targets stores and tracks. When a target’s code mentions another target by name, it depends on that target. The analysis has four stages:
select input -> check studies -> fit meta-analysis -> write summary









Stage
Numbered steps in the script
Targets
Your gap




Select input
1–3
version_file, data_version, dataset_file
None


Check studies
4
studies
None


Fit meta-analysis
5
fit
TODO 1 connects studies to fit


Write summary
6–7
result, summary_file
TODO 2 writes the summary file



The checked studies also feed a second output: the linear regression predictive model from the versioning demonstration. The summary records that model’s version.
check studies -> train and pin predictive model -> model version in the summary






Every target and its dependencies





version_file -> data_version -> dataset_file -> studies -> fit
dataset_file, data_version -> data_provenance
studies, data_provenance, data_version -> predictive_model -> model_pin_files -> model_version
fit, data_provenance, data_version, model_version, pipeline_file -> result -> summary_file
version_file, dataset_file, and summary_file are file targets: targets tracks the contents of the selection file, the pinned RDS file, and the summary CSV. pipeline_file tracks the analysis script and its checksum.



The model uses the raw Pearson correlations and study sample sizes. meta transforms each correlation to Fisher’s z scale and pools the effects with a random-effects model. We use restricted maximum likelihood (REML) to estimate between-study variance and the Hartung–Knapp method for the 95% confidence interval of the pooled correlation. The summary converts the estimate and limits back to the correlation scale. It also records between-study heterogeneity and a 95% prediction interval, which the report lesson explains.
This model treats study summaries as independent and assumes their correlations address a comparable association. Differences in populations, measures, and sampling limit interpretation. This is a worked example of pooling reported effects from the supplied studies (Harrer et al. 2021, sec. 4.2.4).

10.4 Step 3: complete the three gaps
The Results section reports two 95% intervals that answer different questions:

The confidence interval describes uncertainty in the average association across studies. It usually narrows as studies are added.
The prediction interval describes where the true association in a new, comparable study is likely to fall under the model. It adds the between-study variance, \(\tau^2\), so it stays wide when the studies differ.

I² is the percentage of variation in the study estimates that is due to between-study heterogeneity rather than sampling error. Use these definitions to write TODO 2 in your own words.

11.3 Step 2: make a change and predict the rebuild
In workspace/_targets.R, find the fit target. Change method.tau = "REML" to method.tau = "DL" and save the file. The alternative estimator is called DerSimonian–Laird.

file.edit(pipeline_script)

We run the targets pipeline, noting that the results of each step are cached. Modifying fit will invalidate the cache for that target and its dependencies. But other targets will not be re-run.

targets::tar_outdated(script = pipeline_script, store = pipeline_store)
targets::tar_make(script = pipeline_script, store = pipeline_store)
after <- read.csv(summary_path)
rbind(
  REML = before[, c("pooled_r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "tau2")],
  DL = after[, c("pooled_r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "tau2")]
)
after$pooled_r - before$pooled_r

Expect pipeline_file, fit, result, and summary_file to be run again.
The input checks and predictive model branch remain up to date. Both pooled estimates round to 0.363. Switching from REML to DL increases the pooled correlation by about 0.00010 in this dataset. Compare the reported heterogeneity and intervals for the two estimators.

title: 12  GitHub releases, Zenodo and archiving
text:
12.3 Releases on GitHub
A Git commit identifies a repository revision. A GitHub release gives a tagged revision a name and a place for release notes and attached files.
An archiving service such as Zenodo can store a copy of selected files and issue a Digital Object Identifier (DOI). An archive makes the cited files available under the access conditions of that record (Zenodo, n.d.c).
One release ties your pipeline, report source, lockfile, and metadata together at one tagged revision. A reader can then retrieve that exact combination rather than the repository’s latest state. In the workshop repository, preparing a release follows the steps we have used throughout the session:

Record the changes in the CHANGELOG.md and commit that entry.
Tag the commit and publish a release with notes on the releases page.
Publishing the release builds and pushes the RStudio and Binder Docker images.
With Zenodo integration enabled for the repository, Zenodo also archives the tagged files.

12.5 Supplementary: When the data cannot be shared
Open science can include restricted-access data: you can share the methods, code, metadata, and access conditions while restricting the original observations.
Synthetic data generated with synthpop can help others test whether a workflow runs. It does not let them verify findings computed from data that cannot be accessed, and it does not guarantee privacy. The supplementary synthetic data exercise works through an example after the workshop.

12.7 After the workshop: archive your own releases
To archive releases of your own repository, follow Zenodo’s Enable a repository guide:

Connect your GitHub account to Zenodo if it is not already linked.
In Zenodo’s profile menu, select GitHub.
Select Sync now to refresh the list of repositories.
Find the repository you maintain and enable its slider.
Refresh the page and check that the repository is enabled.

Once connected, publishing a new GitHub release triggers automatic archiving in Zenodo. Inspect the resulting version record, its DOI, metadata, and downloadable files after each release. The Sync now control refreshes the repository list; published releases are the events that create new archives.

14.1 Introduction
This supplementary exercise is outside the timed programme and takes about 15 minutes.

14.2 Prepare the study summaries
We read the full 29-study dataset by its recorded pin version, so the exercise starts from the same input as the workshop pipeline.

source("pipelines/workshop_support.R")
use_workshop_book_outputs()

box::use(pins[board_folder, pin_read], utils[read.csv])

source("pipelines/workshop_support.R")
workshop_dir <- workshop_output_dir()
versions <- read.csv(
  file.path(workshop_dir, "dataset-versions.csv"),
  colClasses = "character"
)
full_version <- versions$version[versions$scope == "all"]
stopifnot(length(full_version) == 1L)

data_board <- board_folder(
  file.path(workshop_dir, "data_store"),
  versioned = TRUE
)
health_full <- pin_read(
  data_board, "health_wellbeing", version = full_version
)
stopifnot(nrow(health_full) == 29L)

original <- data.frame(
  population = factor(health_full$population),
  z = atanh(health_full$cor),
  log_n = log(health_full$n)
)

z is the Fisher transformation of the correlation, and log_n is the natural log of the study sample size. The example uses study summaries and leaves out the original study labels and country column.

14.3 Generate synthetic study summaries
We use the CART synthesis method with seed 123, so the run can be repeated in the same environment. We convert the generated values to the original scales and give the new rows synthetic labels. The generated sample sizes describe synthetic rows, not real studies.

  cor = tanh(synthetic$syn$z),

section: 14.4 Try it yourself: pool both datasets
text:
14.4 Try it yourself: pool both datasets
Run the workshop’s random-effects model on the original and the synthetic study summaries, and compare the pooled correlations.

box::use(meta[metacor])

pool_correlations <- function(data) {
  model <- metacor(
    cor = cor,
    n = n,
    studlab = author,
    data = data,
    sm = "ZCOR",
    common = FALSE,
    random = TRUE,
    method.tau = "REML",
    method.random.ci = "HK"
  )
  c(
    studies = model$k,
    pooled_r = tanh(model$TE.random),
    ci_lower = tanh(model$lower.random),
    ci_upper = tanh(model$upper.random)
  )
}

round(
  rbind(
    original = pool_correlations(health_full),
    synthetic = pool_correlations(synthetic_data)
  ),
  3
)

          studies pooled_r ci_lower ci_upper
original       29    0.363    0.309    0.415
synthetic      29    0.359    0.305    0.411


The above code runs on the synthetic table, so a reader without access to restricted data could test that the workflow works. A close match would not verify the original finding, and a difference would not refute it.

14.5 Limits on interpretation and sharing
Ordinary synthesis with synthpop is not a differential privacy guarantee. A privacy claim requires a validated mechanism and privacy accounting (Near and Darais 2021).
Synthetic data also does not confer privacy protection on related models, evaluation results, or metadata.
